period-1/timbuktu.html.title: Timbuktu
period-1/timbuktu.html.description:
As a highly important cultural hotpost, it was developed after Mansa Musa's Hajj, extremely Muslim, and was a critical trade city. Similar to Baghdad, as a core cultural hotspot, it also served as an important place of learning.
Timbuktu also served a practical purpose of legitimizing the Mali Empire, by serving as a beacon of its strength and Muslim identity. Thus, it attracted many other traders from other nations justifying the Mali empire to both foreign and domestic peoples.

period-1/tribute-system.html.title: Tribute System
period-1/tribute-system.html.description:
China gained immense wealth by forcing other nations to pay tribute to them, in goods or money (goods like Champa Rice were accepted as well). They mainly had three major tributary states: Vietnam, Japan, and Korea. By forcing other states to pay tribute, China was able to maintain power and prevent the other states from accumulating too much wealth. The tribute system was based on the idea that China is the cultural, economic, and technological leader of Asia, and as long as tribute states kept paying tribute, that idea was perpetuated and legitimized China’s rule.
An effect of this was that China would sinicize other nations and cause them to change.
Korea would basically become a Chinese clone, adopting Confucianism entirely, and Neo-Confucianism was adopted by Japan and Korea. The Chinese Writing system was adopted by all three as well.
Furthermore, in Japan and Korea (Vietnam resisted), the role of women also shifted due to Confucianism, and these nations became more patriarchal.

period-1/urbanization.html.title: Urbanization
period-1/urbanization.html.description: As trade increased the wealth of nations, (Commercialization), these states would start to have hubs for trade and thus cities would start being created/developed to a larger extent. These new important cities led to a wealth of new opportunities, especially to support a new middle class with specific skills such as artists. Urbanization helped lead to new jobs and increased prosperity.

period-1/yam-system.html.title: Yam System
period-1/yam-system.html.description: The securing of the Mongol empire's trade routes, leading to the Pax Mongolica. These relays made it much safer and cheaper for trade to occur, and these relays helped with communication as well and governance over their massive empire. The relays did not govern trade, instead they secured the trade routes and only taxed merchants using their services slightly - by not controlling trade, and only taxing merchants, trade still occurred and the increased safety overweighed the cost. Thus, the Yam System, by securing trade routes, helped expand the use of trade networks and due to the size of the Mongol empire, helped facilitate cross-regional interactions.

period-1/yuan-dynasty.html.title: Yuan Dynasty
period-1/yuan-dynasty.html.description:
The dynasty that the Mongols created in China, to legitimize themselves as rules while they extracted wealth from China - keep in mind this is a dynasty, they had to follow dynastic rules.
In the Yuan Dynasty, the Mongols sinicized, and didn’t cause major changes to China - the Yuan dynasty adopted Confucian traditions, continuing typical Chinese dynastic traditions. They would follow many Confucian traditions in order to maintain their power and legitimize themselves, ultimately staying out of China. China changed the Mongols, but the Mongols didn’t change China.

period-1/zheng-he-voyages.html.title: Zheng He Voyages
period-1/zheng-he-voyages.html.description:
The Zheng He voyages, during the Ming empire, were voyages to establish trade relations that expanded China’s view of the world, but these voyages were stopped after Zheng He - China isolated itself (Due to Ming Xenophobia & confucianism). However, these voyages were extremely successful, going as far as many of the Swahili Trade States in East Africa.
The Ming dynasty was prosperous at this time and thus the voyages were extravagant, with ships of sizes never seen before. This demonstrated to their tributary states and their population how prosperous and powerful they were, intimidating and also convincing their population not to rebel due to their prosperity/strength. These voyages helped legitimize the Ming Dynasty, yet they were shut down due to confucianist elites (yes I know that's not a word) fearing that this extended view would lead to more radical views from their population

period-2/akbar-the-great.html.title: Akbar the Great
period-2/akbar-the-great.html.description:
One of the greatest Mughal kings, Akbar the Great was extremely religiously tolerant, with a policy of sulh i kul (no, you don't need to know that) a belief system/way of life of acceptance of religions. Some notable law changes were that Shia/Sunni were allowed to both worship in the same mosques, and the abolishment of the Jizya tax completely.
By promoting religious diversity, Akbar limited rebellions due to the majority Hindu population in the Mughal empire, which would have rose up in rebellion under religious limitations from foreigners. These policies led to India becoming a religious hotspot, allowing for religions to mix and spread, such as Sikhism, a merger between Hinduism and Muslim ideas. Without religious tolerance during this period, these cultures would have been unable to mix.

period-2/amsterdam-stock-exchange.html.title: Amsterdam Stock Exchange
period-2/amsterdam-stock-exchange.html.description:
The Amsterdam Stock Exchange created an environment for these joint stock companies to survive - they provided opportunities for common people to invest in these companies, giving them more wealth to be able to conduct business. 
Furthermore, due to the prior existence of the stock exchange, people were already used to investing stock into normal companies, and eventually buying stock into trade voyages would become common as well. Thus, this environment fostered investment into these companies, making the VOC the first companies to successfully achieve a monopoly as a joint stock company (even though it was established after the EIC)

period-2/battle-of-chaldiran.html.title: Battle of Chaldiran
period-2/battle-of-chaldiran.html.description: A battle between the Safavid and the Ottoman empires, which the Ottomans won. This is an example of the religious tension and religious wars due to Sunni vs. Shiites, and is an easy example of clear, direct fighting between these empires. The Ottomans would heavily utilized Gunpowder in order to defeat the Safavid with superior cannon technology. Thus, this battle shows how vital gunpowder was to expansion and conflict between these new empires.

period-2/battle-of-panipat.html.title: Battle of Panipat
period-2/battle-of-panipat.html.description: Similar to the Battle of Chaldiran, an example of how important gunpowder was, without gunpowder, the Delhi Sultanate would collapse under the pressure of the new Mughal empire where the Mughals utilized gunpowder heavily to dominate the Dehli Sultanate.

period-2/black-pepper.html.title: Black Pepper
period-2/black-pepper.html.description: A monopoly on black pepper by the Portuguese, it was one of the major monopolies of the IOB similar to nutmeg and the Dutch. This is a huge change: before, IOB trade was unrestricted and followed the concept of “free trade”, with independent trade-based city-states participating in trade. Monopolies limited and hindered free trade, and changed the I.O.B by introducing economic limitations. This leads to the Portuguese being able to become extremely rich and wealthy and profit off of the pepper trade, helping them catch up to China and the empires in the Middle East.

period-2/british-empire.html.title: British Empire
period-2/british-empire.html.description: The British empire would begin to emerge as a major power in this time period, but was still weaker than the other two dominant nations at the time: Spain and Portugal. They would have major holdings in India and the American colonies, which produced cotton/indigo and tobacco respectively, and would also be one of the first nations to adopt Joint Stock Companies in order to control their colonial holdings. They would only really develop during period 3 when they utilized Opium to gain immense wealth and had major control of China.

period-2/cartaz.html.title: Cartaz
period-2/cartaz.html.description: The trading post empire of the Portuguese was how they “colonized” and controlled the Indian Ocean Basin trade. By forcing ships to purchase a Cartaz, a document stating they were “allowed to trade”, they made money off of the I.O.B. Without one, ships couldn’t trade at their trading ports, and the Portuguese would act as privateers and raid ships. This system would slightly decrease trade in the I.O.B and changed the I.O.B from a "free-trade" system into a more controlled one. However, trade still continued, just with the Portuguese leeching off of its wealth.

period-2/devisherme.html.title: Devisherme
period-2/devisherme.html.description: A system in which young Christian boys were forcibly converted to become Janissaries (converted to become Muslims, and members of the officer class). They could become the elites of Ottoman society, and were a critical part of Ottoman administration. By having a class of people who were indoctrinated in loyalty to the Ottoman empire, who had no other loyalties, the Ottoman empire had a strong system of elites who were able to administrate and manage their empire efficiently without falling victim to power struggles. Furthermore, they were promoted mainly on meritocratic basis, as birth had no effect. Similar to the Mansabdars, this system helped create a meritocracy and helped the ruler maintain direct rule.

period-2/dutch.html.title: Dutch
period-2/dutch.html.description:
The Dutch would utilize their more developed economic and trade systems to accumulate wealth and capital and would also begin their imperial foray.
They would mainly control the Spice Islands, and gain immense wealth by forcibly turning the Banda islands into an export economy. This model would be used in period 3 and period 4 of converting colonies into export colonies, and it was extremely successful to gain immense wealth.

period-2/france.html.title: France
period-2/france.html.description: The most powerful land-based empire of Europe, France would become great under the leadership of the Sun King, Louis XIV. They were mainly notable for utilizing architecture and absolutism to legitimize their government, and also for going into debt and setting the stage for the French Revolution in P3.

period-2/ghulam.html.title: Ghulam
period-2/ghulam.html.description: The Ghulam system was a system in which prisoners of war would be enslaved and used as slave soldiers. This provided an elite military force, and similar to the Mamluks, while they were slaves they were still paid highly and treated well in order to prevent rebellion. They served a similar role to Mamluks and Janissaries, where like in the Devisherme system these soldiers would be indoctrinated in loyalty to the Shah. This gave the Safavid empire one of the first examples of a trained military force, and helped maintain power by keeping the military under direct control of the ruler, and ensured that the military wasn't loyal to aristocratic families

period-2/gold,-god,-glory.html.title: Gold, God, Glory
period-2/gold,-god,-glory.html.description: These were the main motivations for Europeans to engage in maritime trade and develop new maritime empires.Gain money by bypassing Italian and Ottoman middlemen on land-based trade routes, especially for Chinese luxury goods which were still in high demand. Furthermore, find colonies for cash crops/silver/gold, which would also increase the wealth of these new empires.The failure of the crusades and the rise of Muslim empires threatened Christian nation-states and the church, which slowly had less money from tithes due to reduced population believing in the Catholic Church. Furthermore, the Protestant revolution severely weakened the Catholic Church, and Catholic states such as Spain were eager to find new targets to convert to Christianity.With Europe finally become more stabilized and the rise of stronger nation-states that had more direct political control over their governments and nobles, these rising nation states competed against each other for power. Having more colonies meant having more resources and more territory, which helped in the competition between these states

period-2/gunpowder.html.title: Gunpowder
period-2/gunpowder.html.description:
Possibly the single most important military advancement, allowed for the rise of new gunpowder empires which utilized gunpowder heavily in military conquests for expansion.
Gunpowder was imported from China into many other nations, but these nations would innovate heavily and gunpowder technology would determine the winners and losers of P2.

period-2/hacienda-+-encomienda.html.title: Hacienda + Encomienda
period-2/hacienda-+-encomienda.html.description: The hacienda/encomienda systems were systems in which Spain would force labor from indigenous people, supported by their caste system for their plantations and also silver mines. While the Mi’ta system was monthly and a labor tax, the encomienda and hacienda systems were abused systems of slavery, disguised as indentured servitude.

period-2/hall-of-mirrors.html.title: Hall of Mirrors
period-2/hall-of-mirrors.html.description:
A hall created to showcase the power of the Sun King, Louis XIV, and was in the grandiose and extravagant Palace of Versailles.
It's opulence put France into debt, which would eventually lead to many issues later down the line in the French Revolution, but when it was used in the Golden Age of France, it was used for meetings to intimidate nobles and legitimize Louis XIV by demonstrating his immense wealth.

period-2/imperial-examinations.html.title: Imperial Examinations
period-2/imperial-examinations.html.description: These imperial examinations continued from the past, from period 1 (A continuity!). The core governing system of the Qing was still Confucianism, which obviously continued to have similar benefits. Quote from other note: These were meritocratic examinations that anyone could take, leading to the creation of a scholar-official bureaucratic class. However, it was still unbalanced and unfair due to tutoring, much like the SAT and other "standardized" exams today, rich families could afford the tutors necessary, but sometimes poor towns would sponsor someone. By allowing limited social ability, rulers gave commoners a way to improve their status keeping commoners more accepting of their lowered social status (they "deserved" it). However, the prohibitive cost also served to still keep commoners out of higher social levels, and helped keep the rulers in power.

period-2/joint-stock-companies.html.title: Joint Stock Companies
period-2/joint-stock-companies.html.description:
Joint stock companies allowed for more risks to be taken across trade journeys due to distributed capital reducing the risk. Two major ones were created during P2, the British and the Dutch:The VOC and Dutch West Indies Co. gained enough capital to field a military and were able to drive away European competitors in the area like the British. They took over the Spice Islands, especially the Banda islands (due to nutmeg, and caused a genocide there). They leveraged their wealth to essentially operate as an independent nation, where they operated without any oversight.
Due to their profit-seeking nature, they would commit multiple crimes against humanity and use their immense wealth to control the Spice islands, esp. Nutmeg, for most of this period.
Their monopoly over spice was unseen before in the IOB, and would lead to other nations wanting in like the British which would try to take India. However there was a change from previous ideals - instead of shipping nutmeg straight back to Europe, they would sell within the IOB itself for valuable goods first, starting to participate in the lucrative IOB trade which is  a change as previously mercantilist policies led to colonies always shipping back to Europe.The British East India Co. was founded by the British in P.2 BEFORE the Dutch, and they would leverage their wealth to try and take over India. Using their immense wealth and status as a corporation without any state leverage, they quickly made alliances with people against the Mughals and then betrayed them once the Mughal threat was over.
They would then colonize and rule over India, chasing profit ruthlessly through activities such as growing opium, and building multiple trade monopolies and controlling the majority of the shipping back to Britain of luxury Indian and Chinese goods. (also basic commodities like saltpeter).

period-2/kangxi.html.title: Kangxi
period-2/kangxi.html.description: Kangxi would reemphasize Confucianism and turns China inward, only allowing maritime trade in 4 ports. Similar to the Tokugawa Shogunate, it is another example of resistance towards imperial expansion of Europeans by denying them access to their country.

period-2/manila-silver-galleons.html.title: Manila Silver Galleons
period-2/manila-silver-galleons.html.description: A key port in the Phillipines, the Spanish would arrive in Manila and ship silver from Potosi & Huancavelica and carry back luxury goods like porcelain/tea from China, utilizing the new technology of galleons that were able to make longer-distance trips with high amounts of cargo space. The Manila galleons show a change as they show how trade was truly globalized, finally including the Americas inside major trade routes.

period-2/mansabdars.html.title: Mansabdars
period-2/mansabdars.html.description:
The Mansabdars were an elite that was granted tax collection rights by the Mughal king, similar to lesser nobles in the European structure, where these nobles also had to support a military for the Mughal emperors. However, these titles could be taken away, and were not inherited.
This allowed for direct rule by the ruler, and this direct control limited rebellion and promoted stability by limiting the power of the aristocracy.
However, this system would still end up backfiring as the Mansabdars would build up immense power and wealth leading to splinter factions breaking up the Mughal empire.

period-2/maroon-societies.html.title: Maroon Societies
period-2/maroon-societies.html.description:
Slaves would attempt to escape, and they would form new societies that would continue resist slavery militarily directly and act as independent states (political/violent resistance).
However, they would also maintain their culture and preserve African culture in the Americas which was a form of cultural resistance against assimilation as well. Eventually, they would reintegrate into American society and help develop African-American culture.

period-2/millet-system.html.title: Millet System
period-2/millet-system.html.description:
A system where the Ottomans allowed subcommunities to self-govern, such as the Jews, Armenians, and Christians. They allowed them to govern themselves internally, effectively acting as a government within a government.
This religious tolerance meant that when the Ottomans conquered a region, instead of wasting time putting down uprisings due to an unwilling population, they could continue expanding rapidly. This allowed them to expand the reach of their territory tremendously and lowered the risk of rebellions internally from conquered peoples.
The Millet system allowed for many other nation-states to join the Ottoman empire and allowed them to quickly garner support from conquered nations. This led to extremely stable rule in the Ottoman empire, making the Ottoman empire one of the most stable and prosperous land-based empires, developing into the “Ottoman threat” to Europe.

period-2/missionary-activities.html.title: Missionary Activities
period-2/missionary-activities.html.description:
The Catholic Church would attempt to expand their influence in response to the Protestant reformation, especially through the use of Jesuit missionaries.
The Jesuits would be forced to adapt their teachings and scriptures to other cultures, leading to religious syncretism (e.g in China, Spanish Colonies, Pachamama).
Especially in the Spanish colonies, they were extremely prevalent and would focus on conversion of native peoples, relying on syncretism to carry their message across.

period-2/mughal-empire.html.title: Mughal Empire
period-2/mughal-empire.html.description: They would defeat the Delhi sultanate in the Battle of Panipat, and were especially famous for their religious tolerance. Under the rule of religiously tolerant leaders such as Akbar the Great, they would develop new religions such as Sikhism, but their final rulers such as Aurangzeb would be religiously intolerant and lead to the fall of the Mughals. They were important culturally, leading to Muslim rule in Hindu India and thus the aforementioned syncretism, and created pieces of monumental architecture such as the Taj Mahal.

period-2/nutmeg.html.title: Nutmeg
period-2/nutmeg.html.description: Similar to Black Pepper, nutmeg was another monopoly created by the dutch which dramatically shifted I.O.B trade: This is a huge change: before, IOB trade was unrestricted and followed the concept of “free trade”, with independent trade-based city-states participating in trade. Monopolies limited and hindered free trade, and changed the I.O.B by introducing economic limitations. Furthermore, the specific actions that the Dutch took were unique as they converted the Banda islands into an export economy, and in doing so created a genocide via starvation - a negative effect of increased trade.

period-2/ottoman-empire.html.title: Ottoman Empire
period-2/ottoman-empire.html.description: One of the other great powers, only behind the Qing empire (but definitely extremely powerful militarily). Due to its amazing geographic position, they acted as middlemen for Silk Road trade to Italian city states in the Mediterranean. Their markups were what caused Portugal and Spain to seek new sea routes to China for their ever-increasing desire of Chinese luxury goods. They would utilize a strong administration and military system to completely dominate all their neighbors, especially the Safavid empire in the Battle of Chaldiran as a Sunni empire.

period-2/potosi-&-huancavelica.html.title: Potosi & Huancavelica
period-2/potosi-&-huancavelica.html.description:
Mt. Potosi and Mt Huancavelica were the main Spanish silver sources and were a core part of the Spanish colonies’ silver economy. Potosi was a literal mountain of silver, which allowed the Spanish to get rich off of the insatiable need for silver of the Qing.
Mt. Potosi was the source of silver, and Huancavelica was the mercury hub that purified the silver. They heavily used forced labor/slave labor, and the toxic mercury was extremely dangerous leading to continuous importation of slaves.

period-2/prince-henry-the-navigator.html.title: Prince Henry the Navigator
period-2/prince-henry-the-navigator.html.description:
Did not actually explore, but instead was a state sponsor for explorers for Portugal, such as Vasco Da Gama's voyages for the Portuguese. He contributed capital and economic incentive for explorers, which was critical for developing motivation to explore and find new trade routes.
This directly led to the development of new colonies and maritime empires, and Prince Henry and other state sponsors were vital to provide incentive to explorers to discover paths to new colonies.

period-2/pueblo-revolts.html.title: Pueblo Revolts
period-2/pueblo-revolts.html.description:
A revolution by the indigenous population in the Spanish colonies in New Mexico, who actually successfully drove out the Spanish.
It was caused due to forced religious assimilation, and aimed to regain their religious freedoms.
Ultimately, the Spanish returned when the Pueblo people started to run out of food, but the threat of revolt caused them to ease some of the religious restrictions they had previously imposed.

period-2/qing-empire.html.title: Qing Empire
period-2/qing-empire.html.description:
The Qing empire during this time period was still undeniably the single most influential empire in the world, evidenced by the entire world economy being propped up by the silver trade.
However, it's reliance on silver would eventually spell its doom - it would solely import silver, which is not a valuable good while exporting actually valuable luxury goods.
Still, it accumulated immense wealth, and also heavily utilized gunpowder to great effect in small scale conflicts. However, it did not develop to as great an extent of other empires and colonize other nations, only holding onto Tibet as a "colony".

period-2/queen-ana-nzinga.html.title: Queen Ana Nzinga
period-2/queen-ana-nzinga.html.description:
Ruler of the Ndongo and Matmba nations, she would negotiate treaties with the Portuguese and avoided turning the Ndongo and Matamba into other slave nations, fighting and rebelling against the Portuguese throughout her rule.
She is a key example of the African resistance to the slave trade/European colonial expansion, and shows that not every single nation devolved into slavery in Africa in order to win the arms race against other African slave states, with some African nations resisting European influence.

period-2/renaissance.html.title: Renaissance
period-2/renaissance.html.description:
Due to the influence of Dar al-Islam in P1, bringing in influence through Al-Andalus and the Crusades, Europe was undergoing a period of intellectual flourishing that encouraged technological development. This helped Europe adapt quickly to new maritime technologies that helped navigation and helped Europe catch up the the East.
Furthermore, the environment of discovery and intellectual development led to many explorers and "discoverers", which led to more voyages by nations to help create maritime empires.

period-2/russian-empire.html.title: Russian Empire
period-2/russian-empire.html.description: Russia during this time period was weakened by internal strife and the continued influence of the Mongols, but would begin attempts at Westernization and modernization during P2 which was somewhat successful for the elites, such as the Table of Ranks. Especially under the reign of Peter the Great, who created St. Petersburg as a "Window to the West", and aimed to westernize, some reforms were attempted. However, the overall social system remained the same with serfdom being a core part of the economy of Russia. The lack of modernization and westernization for most of Russia made Russia unable to westernize and industrialize in P3.

period-2/safavid-empire.html.title: Safavid Empire
period-2/safavid-empire.html.description:
Mainly notable for the fact that they are the only Shi'a gunpowder empire in Period 2, where every other nation is Sunni.
They were extremely similar to the other Muslim empires, utilizing many of the same strategies for administration, military, and economic control. The only major difference is their Shi'ism, which caused them to continuously be in conflict with the other Sunni nations around them and also led to religious intolerance.

period-2/silver.html.title: Silver
period-2/silver.html.description:
Possibly the most single most important resource in period 2, the Qing dynasty/Ming dynasty's single whip taxation system made it the official currency of China. This helped the Qing maintain control over its economic system, at the cost of requiring silver for all economic transactions.
Due to the Qing overvaluing silver as it was necessary for internal trade, it warped the world economy around it, and the rise of new silver sources led to inflation in the global economy as the Qing dumped luxury goods onto the market in exchange for American silver.

period-2/sociedad-de-castas.html.title: Sociedad de Castas
period-2/sociedad-de-castas.html.description:
The creation of new social structures in order to justify the Spanish use of the indigenous population, it was promoted heavily by the Spanish settlers.
It was extremely detailed and government structured, with more and more indigenous blood being classified as lower class, and provided a racist and social justification for abuse of workers.
As the colonies became more diverse, especially with African slaves, the social structure became increasingly more complex in order to continue supporting the whites/Spanish at the top of the social hierarchy.
This system was created mainly in part due to the outnumbered Spanish: at 20% of the population, they were outnumbered and needed this clear social structure to limit the power of other groups and to prevent potential uprisings/rebellions if they gained too much power.**

period-2/spain.html.title: Spain
period-2/spain.html.description:
The most powerful maritime empire in period 2, but significantly declined afterwards. They had most of their colonial holdings in the Americas, notably the Caribbean and Latin America.
They would produce many cash crops such as sugar, coffee, cacao, but none of these were really as important as silver. Spain is important for introducing one of the biggest sources of American silver, and by trading it to China, would finally create a global trading network.
However, they over relied on silver, and when inflation hit, their wealth would suddenly collapse especially due to a lack of diversification and economic development due to multiple wars.

period-2/stono-rebellion.html.title: Stono Rebellion
period-2/stono-rebellion.html.description:
The largest slave rebellion in the British colonies, in South Carolina slaves aimed to collect arms and march to Florida where the Spanish offered them freedom.
Ultimately, the rebellion was put down and led to harsher restrictions, but is still an example of attempted resistance against the British empire.

period-2/table-of-ranks.html.title: Table of Ranks
period-2/table-of-ranks.html.description:
The Table of Ranks was a meritocratic system in which service to the Tsar and ability/skills were theoretically the only way in which to climb the ranks. This meant that money/influence in the empire couldn’t get unskilled family members into powerful positions. However, it was slowly undermined later on, as Tsars made the requirements more lenient.
This helped the Tsar maintain their power easily as noble uprisings were more difficult as the Tsar maintained direct control of the social/political structure. Thus, this also allowed the Tsar to gain a highly skilled administrative structure.
This allowed the Russian Empire to have a lot of skilled governors/leaders/bureaucrats to administrate throughout the empire, and it also centralized power, as aristocrats/noble families couldn’t leverage their power as much if it was directly granted from the Tsar.

period-2/taj-mahal.html.title: Taj Mahal
period-2/taj-mahal.html.description:
Taj Mahal was a huge mausoleum, being built at huge cost at the height of the Mughal empire under Shah Jahan.
The immense Taj Mahal legitimized the Mughal empire by demonstrating their immense wealth and prosperity to their population, showing how prosperous the empire was.
It also demonstrates religious syncretism, as it merges both Persian (read: Muslim) and Indian elements of architecture.

period-2/tax-farming.html.title: Tax Farming
period-2/tax-farming.html.description:
The Iltizam, tax farming under the Ottomans, where the rights to taxing a certain piece of land were auctioned off and sold to the highest bidder. The Iltizam allowed the Ottomans to gain money to fund their extensive military campaigns, but eventually the ottomans would have to cut back and find other ways to raise cash, as slowly they lost more and more revenue Similar to Zamindars, sometimes sacrifices had to be made for effective taxation and economic growth.The Safavids also had similar methods of tax farming. Similar to the Ottomans and Mughals, they would grant local leaders the right to tax in exchange for quick cash.
See Mansabdars and Zamindars.

period-2/tokugawa-shogunate.html.title: Tokugawa Shogunate
period-2/tokugawa-shogunate.html.description:
The Sakoku edict of 1635 was an example of resistance to European imperialist expansion, as Japan closes themselves off to foreigners completely (except for the less-religious Dutch).
This edict is an example of resistance because it shows Asian countries preventing Europeans from enroaching onto their territory, and demonstrates how European powers are not powerful enough to force the Eastern nations directly.

period-2/yasak-system.html.title: Yasak System
period-2/yasak-system.html.description: The Yasak collection was a tax collection system in Russia, of tribute that amounted to basically fur taxation. This taxation policy was created because of the fur trade from Russia to Europe - without the fur tribute, Russia couldn’t have enough fur to trade with Western Europe for goods that they needed. By constructing a stable taxation system, similar to the Qing single whip system, it kept the economy more stable and helped create a "unified currency" for taxation, helping the Russian Empire maintain stronger economic control over their empire.

period-2/zamindars.html.title: Zamindars
period-2/zamindars.html.description:
Extremely similar to the Mansabdars, but they were hereditary and only served as intermediaries between the people and the ruler. Similar to the Mansabdars, they became corrupt and splintered the Mughal empire. Essentially they served the same role as the Mansabdars in terms of tax collection, allowing the empire to be able to collect taxes over their huge territory.
Thus, they show that the Mughals had to sacrifice some amount of centralized control for effective taxation policies, similar to the Yasak System where furs were taken as tax but natives had different methods of tax collection.

period-3/balkan-nationalism.html.title: Balkan Nationalism
period-3/balkan-nationalism.html.description:
Serbs, Greeks, and Romanians used ethnic identity and Russian Pan-Slavic support to break away from the Ottoman Empire, and created new nation states. These new nation states that rose out of the Ottoman empire heavily emphasized nationalism and a unified language and culture, creating a strong enough national identity to fight for independence.
As the Ottomans failed to industrialize, ethnic groups used nationalism as a tool in order to fight for their own independence. However, this created instability in Europe, and these new states became the site of proxy wars (Russia vs. Austria). This shifted the focus of global conflict back to Europe instead of over colonies, directly providing the spark for the alliance system that caused World War I.

period-3/berlin-conference.html.title: Berlin Conference
period-3/berlin-conference.html.description:
The Berlin Conference, and the Scramble for Africa, was a meeting where European nations met in order to divide up Africa to exploit it as colonies. Notably, Belgium got the entire Congo and turned it into a slave export economy.
The Berlin Conference is an example of how Europeans would begin to formalize the theft of non-European land, and aim to prevent European war. This is different and a huge change - in P2, these meetings could not happen due to Europeans being much weaker militarily and economically. However, in P3, the increased power of Europeans gave them the power to dictate borders without considering the populations involved due to their overwhelming power.
The artificial borders drawn at Berlin, ignoring ethnic/linguistic lines, became the primary cause of post-colonial state instability and civil war in Africa in P4.

period-3/boxer-rebellion.html.title: Boxer Rebellion
period-3/boxer-rebellion.html.description:
A 1900 uprising by the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists. They targeted "foreign devils" (engineers, missionaries) and rejected westerners and western modernization in favor of Confucianism and cultural purity, trying to keep their cultural identity independent. Ultimately failed due to Cixi’s initial promotion of the rebellion and then secondary betrayal, where she asked foreigners to stop the Boxer Rebellion (which increased foreign involvement in the Boxer Rebellion).
Also an example of anti-westernization and industrialization as well, as the Boxer rebellion aimed to remove Western influences in general (imperialism and industrialization)

period-3/british-raj.html.title: British Raj
period-3/british-raj.html.description:
After the Sepoy rebellion, the British would assume direct rule with the failure of the BEIC to maintain power. This transition from a commercial to political economy had long-lasting changes on India.
The British would increase in racism and significantly favor the British in India, especially with reforms and policies. This would increase the amount of resistance by the native population, resulting in the Indian National Congress being formed which would eventually lead to the downfall of the British Raj.
In a sense, the British Raj was going back to "old" imperialism, by focusing more on political rule and governance.

period-3/capitalism.html.title: Capitalism
period-3/capitalism.html.description:
Adam Smith argued for supply and demand to control the market and to leave it alone (laissez faire), instead of using mercantilism which argued for strict government control.
This suggestion allowed nations to reconsider their economic theories and this led to some colonies like the U.S becoming angry with strict government regulations that would end up being inferior under this new economic governing style, leading to revolutions.
This led to a belief of more free-market economics and reduced interference by governments, leading to enterprises with poor working conditions and low regulation and worker protection.
Capitalism ended up being a huge change, replacing mercantilism as the dominant economic system. The promotion of free trade and competition led to the rise of more companies and increased amounts of trade, allowing some to get extremely wealthy.

period-3/cherokee-nation.html.title: Cherokee Nation
period-3/cherokee-nation.html.description:
Created a written constitution and court system, and managed to sue Georgia in Worcester vs. Georgia, yet they were still removed in the Trail of Tears, but they were partially successful in their goals.
They would resist against imperialism by adopting Western influences and Western ideologies. By blending in and becoming a Western nation, it was far easier to succeed if they fit easily into existing Western ideologies and used “Western technologies” (democratic advancements like constitutions).
However, the deck was stacked against them, and while they won hypothetically, they would still get removed due to the inequality built into the system.

period-3/consumerism.html.title: Consumerism
period-3/consumerism.html.description:
Higher wages/less work for the middle class lead to consumers, and consumerism (buying things), with the rise of things such as department stores and theatres to help spend money. The new middle class not only had more money, but had more things they could buy with said money.
The rise of consumerism also improved the economy by leading to more spending and also to increased demand for more products to spend money on.
Consumerism was a huge change, from only a select few people being able to spend money on non-survival tasks, now to having the entire middle class being able to afford small luxuries.

period-3/economic-imperialism.html.title: Economic Imperialism
period-3/economic-imperialism.html.description:
Economic imperialism is taking over a country using economics instead of directly controlling them militarily, which is much better for PR and also doesn’t cost as much. Many nations such as India become single-export economies and economically dependent on a single buyer, in India’s case cotton to the U.K leaving them economically dependent on a single material and weakening their economy (e.g if demand dropped, India's economy would be devastated).
This strategy was used heavily by European imperialistic nations for their ambitions, such as in India, where the British forced India to create cotton and opium.
However, sometimes it was supply side (force India to sell cotton), which made them economically dependent on British to buy cotton, or sometimes it was demand-side (China), where they became the chief supplier of some good like opium and controlling them through that method.
Remember - colonies didn't shift to become export economies, they were forced to become export/import economies, and economic imperialism is still imperialism with military control.

period-3/enlightenment-rhetoric.html.title: Enlightenment Rhetoric
period-3/enlightenment-rhetoric.html.description:
Most states would heavily utilize Enlightenment Rhetoric in order to encourage revolutions, with many of the founding documents utilizing Enlightenment rhetoric to emphasize and prove their ideas of independence.
America's Declaration of Independence (Life, Liberty, Happiness = natural rights, social contract) and Constitution (3 branches) are both filled with references to Enlightenment ideals, and Common Sense was filled with Enlightenment ideals as well.
France's Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen was similar as well, and influenced the Haitian Declaration of Independence. Both of these also had references to Enlightenment ideals.
Simon Bolivar's "Letter from Jamaica" also includes thoughts on self-governance as well.

period-3/ethiopia.html.title: Ethiopia
period-3/ethiopia.html.description:
Ethiopia would defeat the Italians and maintain independence, winning by using state monopolies to purchase modern weaponry from France and Russia to help defend Ethiopia.
Using diplomacy and allowing some concessions, and being a Christian nation, Emperor Menelik successfully protected Ethiopia from normal justifications of imperialism allowing him to gain allies or at least neutral nations to fight the Italians on an equal footing, and with modern weaponry was able to win.
Menelik II proved that the only way to resist an industrial power was to become a centralized state with industrial weapons, which thus prevented Ethiopia from being partitioned.

period-3/factories.html.title: Factories
period-3/factories.html.description: Factories allowed for increase of specialized labor and huge efficiency and labor costs reduction, and were possible with the rise of Fossil Fuels providing a better energy source and new machines. They achieved this through the assembly line, allowing for increased division of labor, and standardization of tools and parts allowing for easy fixing and consistent results (due to guns). Factories caused worse working conditions, due to the transition of individual specialists to being cheaper massed labor, which was worse for workers overall. It improved economic growth but large enterprises would replace skilled labor with mass unskilled labor and with have extremely low wages due to low regulations.

period-3/fossil-fuels.html.title: Fossil Fuels
period-3/fossil-fuels.html.description:
Fossil fuel revolution was the change from using other fuels and using more coal and oil for the industrial revolution, leading to fuel as an important resource. Fossil fuels powered the industrial revolution by providing a strong power source for all of the fancy new machines.
It was led by Britain due to cheap easy coal supplies close to the surface. Coal became utilized more often in industrial applications whereas before it was mainly for heating and not a huge industry.

period-3/france.html.title: France
period-3/france.html.description:
The French revolution stemmed out of extreme debt and inequality. It began as a peasant's rebellion against the monarchy, and ultimately didn't achieve much.
While there was a lot of political turmoil, especially with executions by the new revolutionary governments of the entire monarchy and all dissidents of the new government as well, it ultimately devolved back into absolutism with Napoleon Bonaparte taking power as an emperor.
While Napoleon enacted some beneficial laws to turn France into a meritocracy, the social structure remained relatively similar with only increased social mobility in the military and bureaucracy.

period-3/germany.html.title: Germany
period-3/germany.html.description:
With the rise of Nationalism, Bismarck would politically unify Germany and help unify the state of Germany for the first time. He would implement a variety of modernization policies and social reforms and help modernize Germany's military. His use of realpolitik, disregarding morals and ideals for practical solutions contributed to rampant militarization and alliances, contributing to German leaders' ideologies in both the first and second world wars.
The rise of new states, similar to Italy, would lead to the desire for new colonies as well as these states sought to form empires and catch up. However, these states would not be able to form empires in America/Asia, leading to the Berlin Conference to take over Africa

period-3/haiti.html.title: Haiti
period-3/haiti.html.description:
The Haitian revolution was led mainly by the efforts of Toussain Louverture, led against France. It remains the only successful slave revolution, and while they were shackled by extended debt they did gain independence.
It was inspired by the French Revolution, and they succeeded by playing the British and French off of each other (extremely successful). They had to make a single large down payment, but unlike China's war reparations, this was merely for capital and had no interest paid on it.
Haiti is notable for being one of the revolutions that truly changed the social structure, by removing slaves entirely. Unlike other revolutions which only changed political power, Haiti truly reformed the social order.

period-3/imperialism.html.title: Imperialism
period-3/imperialism.html.description:
Imperialism in this period would become new imperialism, with many changes - increased economic motive, different justifications for imperialism, and new/different states that became powerful. New Imperialism gained an emphasis on raw materials for manufacturing. Now, imperialistic states had the capability to actually grow their own economies instead of relying on trade, and thus focused on acquiring the raw materials necessary to produce their products. Furthermore, new imperialism relied on new justifications such as Social Darwinism, and focused more on civilizing rather than religious justifications.
New states also became powerful in the new imperialism era, especially Italy/Germany which would become new nations in this period. Furthermore, Spain and Portugal were not as powerful, with the British Empire being the strongest empire in this period.

period-3/inequality.html.title: Inequality
period-3/inequality.html.description:
With the rise of Capitalism and increased economic expansion, some social classes gained more than others. The lower classes stayed relatively the same, trading in agricultural jobs for industrial ones, and in some sectors worsened - for example, families drifted apart as child laborers worked in different factories from their parents.
However, for the middle class and upper classes, they would benefit greatly from the industrial revolution, increasing in wealth dramatically. They would treat lower classes poorly however, employing Social Darwinism to justify their higher status compared to the lower working class.

period-3/issac-newton.html.title: Issac Newton
period-3/issac-newton.html.description:
Writer of the Principia, he's notable for helping start the scientific revolution - the technologies in the scientific revolution were used for the Industrial revolution. Furthermore, the idea of empiricism would be used in the Enlightenment as well.
The same scientific ideas that were used in the Principia, utilizing deductive reasoning, natural laws that affect all things, and using reason/tests over belief would be reapplied to government and lead to revolutions.

period-3/italy.html.title: Italy
period-3/italy.html.description:
With the rise of Nationalism, Italy would unify as a single state for the first time. Under the leadership of the Count of Cavour, Italy finally formed an independent state for the first time and he utilized military campaigns and the population's desire for a public identity to rise to power.
The rise of new states, similar to Germany, would lead to the desire for new colonies as well as these states sought to form empires and catch up. However, these states would not be able to form empires in America/Asia, leading to the Berlin Conference to take over Africa

period-3/john-locke.html.title: John Locke
period-3/john-locke.html.description: John Locke was one of the key leaders of the Enlightenment, spreading many ideas notably the idea of a Social Contract and Natural Rights, and contributed a lot to the early Enlightenment and created much of the novel ideas around government and government control. John Locke is important for being a trailblazing philosopher who developed a lot of ideas on governments and society, and led to the rise of more Enlightenment thinkers.

period-3/latin-america.html.title: Latin America
period-3/latin-america.html.description:
The entirety of Latin America underwent many revolutions, but overall did not change the social structure for the majority of the population.
The key revolutionary leader, Simon Bolivar, went through most of Latin America and helped them fight for their independence, aiming to create a Gran Colombia (but that ultimately failed).
The social structure of Latin America, with the Sociedad de Castas still remained similar but just without Peninsulares.
Latin America, would eventually devolve into independent states without a Gran Colombia, and Caudillos (military leaders) would form Juntas (regional dictatorships), leading to instability and difficulties to modernize and improve economically.

period-3/luddites.html.title: Luddites
period-3/luddites.html.description:
The Luddites were workers protesting against machines "stealing their jobs", and consisted of weavers who raided factories and destroyed technological machines.
The British and other governments would crack down heavily instead of constructing policies and regulations to protect workers, worsening inequality. They would continue this policy of aggressively attacking workers, thus stalling reforms.
Thus, the Luddites show how the industrial revolution's inequality caused fear among workers and highlights attempts by workers to resist the industrial revolution in order to avoid the inequality that came with factory work.

period-3/mahdist-revolt.html.title: Mahdist Revolt
period-3/mahdist-revolt.html.description:
After defeating the Ottoman/Egyptians at Khartoum, Muhammad Ahmad built an Islamic state and used religion to gain control over Sudan but ultimately lost. This was also fueled due to the slave trade, with the Egyptian abolition of slavery leading to economic downturn. Muhammad would become the Mahdi, a religious leader, and act similar to Muhammed himself to incite rebellion and establish his new Islamic state.
Similar to other examples of resistance, religion was utilized as a unifying factor.
However, in this situation there was a huge economic incentive, namely the loss of the slave trade playing an important role in economic incentive for rebellion.

period-3/maji-maji-rebellion.html.title: Maji Maji Rebellion
period-3/maji-maji-rebellion.html.description: Triggered by forced labor for cotton production in German East Africa, rebels used maji (sacred water) and believed they would be protected against German bullets. Ultimately failed. They would lose due to the Maxim gun being able to decimate their warriors and without machine guns of their own, they were easily wiped out. However, they were successful in unifying utilizing religion, similar to the Xhosa Cow-Killing Movement, but it was different due to their direct military confrontation. In the end, both outcomes were the same: failed rebellion.

period-3/mary-wollstonecraft.html.title: Mary Wollstonecraft
period-3/mary-wollstonecraft.html.description:
One of the first to push for women’s rights during this time period, she's one of the founding feminist philosophers and well known for writing A Vindication of the Rights of Women. Her early ideas inspired other feminist thinkers and kickstarted the first wave of feminism, which would eventually lead to more thought about the rights of women.
Her work is important because it helped sow the seeds of feminism, which would help lead to other thinkers and protesters which would culminate in P4.

period-3/middle-class.html.title: Middle Class
period-3/middle-class.html.description:
The rise of the middle class was a huge industrial trend, as the middle class previously didn’t exist in such numbers. But with new factories, new jobs emerged such as teachers, bankers, etc. as money and the economy shifted to become more privatized and more capitalist, middlemen such as bankers became more common.
The rise of the middle class was a huge social change --> before, the middle class was much smaller, but with the industrial revolution, many could become wealthy essentially creating an entirely new social class.

period-3/montesquieu.html.title: Montesquieu
period-3/montesquieu.html.description: Montesquieu was a French philosopher who developed the system of government of checks and balances, which was used in the United States's revolution and helped lay the groundwork for current democratic systems. His ideas surrounding checks and balances and the seperation of powers influenced modern democratic governments heavily, and helped many states see the potential of having a more equal form of government with a weaker monarchy, motivating revolutions and helping revolutions gain a stable political structure.

period-3/opium-wars.html.title: Opium Wars
period-3/opium-wars.html.description: The opium wars were conflicts sparked by British exportation of opium into China to fix their trade imbalance, leading to unequal treaties such as the Treaty of Nanking. The opium wars are clear examples of how industrialized nations utilized their superior military might in order to force lesser-industrialized states into unfavorable trade agreements, utilizing Economic Imperialism to their advantage to take over countries economically. It also shows how China was still economically one of the most powerful states during this time period even with a lack of industrialization - the British still imported goods from China, and wanted their luxury goods.

This is different and a huge change - in P2, these meetings could not happen due to Europeans being much weaker militarily and economically. However, in P3, the increased power of Europeans gave them the power to dictate borders without considering the populations involved due to their overwhelming power. The artificial borders drawn at Berlin, ignoring ethnic/linguistic lines, became the primary cause of post-colonial state instability and civil war in Africa in P4.Berlin ConferenceEconomic imperialism is taking over a country using economics instead of directly controlling them militarily, which is much better for PR and also doesn’t cost as much. Many nations such as India become single-export economies and economically dependent on a single buyer, in India’s case cotton to the U.K leaving them economically dependent on a single material and weakening their economy (e.g if demand dropped, India's economy would be devastated). This strategy was used heavily by European imperialistic nations for their ambitions, such as in India, where the British forced India to create cotton and opium. However, sometimes it was supply side (force India to sell cotton), which made them economically dependent on British to buy cotton, or sometimes it was demand-side (China), where they became the chief supplier of some good like opium and controlling them through that method. Remember - colonies didn't shift to become export economies, they were forced to become export/import economies, and economic imperialism is still imperialism with military control.Economic Imperialism
Factories allowed for increase of specialized labor and huge efficiency and labor costs reduction, and were possible with the rise of Fossil Fuels providing a better energy source and new machines. They achieved this through the assembly line, allowing for increased division of labor, and standardization of tools and parts allowing for easy fixing and consistent results (due to guns). Factories caused worse working conditions, due to the transition of individual specialists to being cheaper massed labor, which was worse for workers overall. It improved economic growth but large enterprises would replace skilled labor with mass unskilled labor and with have extremely low wages due to low regulations.FactoriesFossil fuel revolution was the change from using other fuels and using more coal and oil for the industrial revolution, leading to fuel as an important resource. Coal became utilized more often in industrial applications whereas before it was mainly for heating and not a huge industry.Fossil FuelsSteamships and railroads lowered costs and increased the speed of travel, especially for larger cargos and allowed for reach upriver, where before it was more difficult. Canals (Suez/Panama) created shortcuts for global trade, connecting oceans and cutting months off voyages. The rise of new transportation methods lowered costs for trade and production, making it even cheaper to produce goods and trade, leading to huge corporations and increased economic growth.
They also supported imperialism, as steamships were extremely valuable for empires due to their ability to sail upriver and allowed for greater reach and penetration into countries. This is similar to Quinine (and other technologies), which allowed for deeper penetration into tropical environments due to their prevention of malaria.Transportation
With the rise of imperialism and Capitalism, money also needed to be managed much more efficiently. Building off of joint stock companies such as VOC and EIC, stocks became more common. Limited Liability Companies also became common as well, where you only ever lose as much money as you put into it - e.g if a company goes into debt they can only try to use the money you paid through stocks, not your own assets. The rise of these new methods of management allowed for much lower risk leading to markets that were more conducive to foreign investment, protecting investors and leading to more capital. this led to larger companies, e.g HSBC and Unilever.Transational BusinessRampant industrialization with complete disregard for waste and industrial byproducts eventually led to pollution.

The rise of pollution shows how the industrial revolution changed how we interacted with the environment by giving humans more power to change the environment. PollutionThe rise of the middle class was a huge industrial trend, as the middle class previously didn’t exist in such numbers. But with new factories, new jobs emerged such as teachers, bankers, etc. as money and the economy shifted to become more privatized and more capitalist, middlemen such as bankers became more common. The rise of the middle class was a huge social change --> before, the middle class was much smaller, but with the industrial revolution, many could become wealthy essentially creating an entirely new social class.Middle ClassWriter of the Principia, he's notable for helping start the scientific revolution - the technologies in the scientific revolution were used for the Industrial revolution. Furthermore, the idea of empiricism would be used in the Enlightenment as well. The British and other governments would crack down heavily instead of constructing policies and regulations to protect workers, worsening inequality. They would continue this policy of aggressively attacking workers, thus stalling reforms. Thus, the Luddites show how the industrial revolution's inequality caused fear among workers and highlights attempts by workers to resist the industrial revolution in order to avoid the inequality that came with factory work.LudditesThe Tanzimat Reforms were a series of radical reforms that attempted to modernize the state, which largely failed due to internal resistance by the religious authority (ulama) and also from Janissaries - both groups resisted heavily and thus most reforms failed to achieve their goals. Ultimately failed due to Cixi’s initial promotion of the rebellion and then secondary betrayal, where she asked foreigners to stop the Boxer Rebellion (which increased foreign involvement in the Boxer Rebellion). Also an example of anti-westernization and industrialization as well, as the Boxer rebellion aimed to remove Western influences in general (imperialism and industrialization)Boxer Rebellion

period-3/quinine-(and-other-technologies.description: The invention of multiple technologies due to the industrial revolution made it easier to establish colonies. Quinine, an ingredient in tonic water, helps protect against malaria and thus helped empires penetrate deeper inland in tropical regions. Steamships helped sailors sail upriver and utilize rivers/waterways to explore and conquer. New weapons such as the maxim gun (also Gatling before) and enfield rifle decimated populations without modern weaponry and led to clean defeats militarily - just one soldier with a maxim gun could kill an entire village

period-3/regulations.html.title: Regulations
period-3/regulations.html.description:
Due to poor working conditions, there would be multiple waves of reform in order to push for improved living conditions in these new industrialized countries.
The 1st wave of reform focused on fixes to severe injustices, such as child labor, sanitation, etc. while the second wave focused on social reforms and public education to prevent the Marxist revolution and to limit public unrest.
Public education and the right to vote were also expanded upon in order to prevent the threat of a revolt.
Reform efforts were assisted by the threat of Marxist revolution, which was a serious threat for most nations who wanted to keep their power - demonstrated in the Russian Revolution (not this period though).

period-3/seneca-falls.html.title: Seneca Falls
period-3/seneca-falls.html.description:
A landmark convention, one of the first official gatherings for women’s rights, where key thinkers like Elizabeth Cady Stanton would join together and draft a revised declaration of independence that included women.
This key landmark event would help spark other grassroots movements, and is a turning point where feminism starts becoming more organized, instead of individual people, it becomes a single large group pushing for equality and independence, which helps it gain political power and helps advance the cause.

period-3/sepoy-mutiny.html.title: Sepoy Mutiny
period-3/sepoy-mutiny.html.description:
An uprising of Indian soldiers (Sepoys) over the use of rifle cartridges greased with cow/pig fat. Involved the restoration of the Mughal Emperor as a figurehead of resistance that ultimately failed but had a lot of support, which showed the U.K how tenuous their rule over India was. There was no evidence that the cartridges were indeed greased with cow fat, and thus it shows how willing the Sepoys were to rebel.
This was a pivotal moment that ended the British East India Company's rule, establishing the Raj system. It forced the British government to take over completely, resulting in a more rigid, racially segregated bureaucracy and a permanent shift from commercial to imperial administration, which was a huge shift from exploitation for economic incentive to imperial and political incentive.

period-3/sino-japanese-war.html.title: Sino-Japanese War
period-3/sino-japanese-war.html.description:
Japan would also join the ranks of empires, with many expansionist policies such as the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars and would establish their dominance by defeating them both.
These successes would create a vicious cycle of nationalism fueling imperialism, as their successes fueled nationalism and created an Anti-Western identity (leading to their actions in WWII).
These wars established Japan as a new imperialist state on par with Europeans and show how nationalism fueled new imperialism.

period-3/social-contract.html.title: Social Contract
period-3/social-contract.html.description:
The social contract significantly influenced other revolutions and revolutionary rhetoric. It was a philosophical idea that individuals consent to rule, and that they can remove their consent at any time.
This groundbreaking idea encouraged revolutions, and delegitimized governments that solely relied on religious hierarchy. Thus, rulers should not use religion and instead use their actions and policies as justification for ruling their population.
Due to higher literacy rates and the printing press, revolutions such as the American Revolution or the French revolution referenced this idea when pushing the issue of independence, stating that their rulers had infringed upon their rights.

period-3/social-darwinism.html.title: Social Darwinism
period-3/social-darwinism.html.description:
Social Darwinism became a scientific way to justify imperialism, and the spread of Liberalism and Christianity played a role in moral justifications for conquest.
Social Darwinism represents a shift from religious to biological “destiny” as a justification for imperial rule. With new tools of science, they could frame imperial rule as a natural law of "survival of the fittest," Western nations managed to convince populations to embrace Enlightenment ideals at home while also participating in colonialism in other nations.

period-3/socialism.html.title: Socialism
period-3/socialism.html.description:
Poor working conditions and capitalism would inspire Karl Marx to write the Communist Manifesto, and lead eventually to communism.
Due to the poor working conditions in many areas of the world, he would attempt to encourage workers to rise up in a workers' revolution. Some states would lead communist revolutions in period 4, but his ideas were already being spread and disseminated.
Note that this happens at the end of P3!

period-3/tabula-rasa.html.title: Tabula Rasa
period-3/tabula-rasa.html.description: One of John Locke's ideas, that man is a blank slate without any innate knowledge and preconceptions. This challenged religious legitimization, stating that no man was born with the right to rule over anyone else. The belief in Tabula Rasa was a stepping stone to other ideas in fields of psychology, sociology, and politics, and helped shape ideas on education and nature vs. nurture. All of these ideas weakened ideas behind birthright, which weakened kings and made it easier to rebel.

period-3/ulama-vs.-tanzimat-reforms.html.description:
The Tanzimat Reforms were a series of radical reforms that attempted to modernize the state, which largely failed due to internal resistance by the religious authority (ulama) and also from Janissaries - both groups resisted heavily and thus most reforms failed to achieve their goals.

period-3/united-states.html.title: United States
period-3/united-states.html.description:
Notable for being the first revolution, and was actually successful against the British Empire (which significantly weakens it). They utilized John Locke's ideas heavily in order to gain independence. Due to a weakening of the British empire due to the 7 years' war, they took advantage of the opportunity to fight for independence.
With the publication of Common Sense, they would heavily utilize Enlightenment rhetoric to argue for their case, which can be seen in the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence. Socially, things remained the same. Rich white landowners still hold most of the power, but this is a step forward and this inspires other revolutions later on.

period-3/xhosa-cow-killing-movement.html.title: Xhosa Cow-Killing Movement
period-3/xhosa-cow-killing-movement.html.description:
A disease spread by European Cattle led to a religious prophecy and the belief in Millenarianism, believing that all things would be changed after the killing of all of the Xhosa cattle, which led to widespread famine and starvation.
While it was unsuccessful, it shows how religion could play a significant role in unifying Africans together to attempt to defend themselves against western imperialism.
Africans during this time period would heavily utilize religion as a way to unify their population in opposition to Western imperialism - oftentimes this failed, but there were many, many attempts.
